prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Temporal Proximity Alone, Absent Unusually Suggestive Timing, Cannot Establish the Causal Link Required for a Retaliation Claim.**

To establish a prima facie case of retaliation, a plaintiff must show (1) protected activity, (2) an adverse employment action, and (3) a causal connection between the two. *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 300 (3d Cir. 2007); *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 500 (3d Cir. 1997). Plaintiff's claim fails at the third element. The only evidence of causation is the sequence of events: [Plaintiff] engaged in protected activity on [date], and [Defendant] took the challenged action on [date]. Under settled Third Circuit law, that sequence does not support an inference of causation unless the interval is unusually suggestive of retaliatory motive.

**A. The governing standard demands unusually suggestive timing.**

This Court has repeatedly held that temporal proximity can support causation by itself only when it is "unusually suggestive." *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004); *Krouse*, 126 F.3d at 503–04. *Jalil v. Avdel Corp.*, 873 F.2d 701, 708 (3d Cir. 1989), illustrates the narrow category of cases that qualify: a discharge two days after the employer received notice of the protected activity. The Supreme Court has likewise recognized that temporal proximity can serve as evidence of causality only when it is "very close," and that even a three- or four-month gap is insufficient. *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001). That caution carries added weight because Title VII retaliation claims require but-for causation. *Univ. of Tex. Sw. Med. Ctr. v. Nassar*, 570 U.S. 338, 360 (2013).

**B. Where the timing is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff needs additional evidence.**

When the interval is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff must point to other evidence "gleaned from the record as a whole" that supports an inference of retaliatory animus. *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 280–81 (3d Cir. 2000). Such evidence may include a pattern of antagonism following the protected activity, inconsistent explanations, or comparator evidence. *Id.*; *Lichtenstein v. Univ. of Pittsburgh Med. Ctr.*, 691 F.3d 294, 307 (3d Cir. 2012). Timing alone does not suffice. In *LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Community Center Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 232–33 (3d Cir. 2007), this Court held that a gap of three months between the protected activity and the adverse action, without more, could not create an inference of causation. *See also Thomas v. Town of Hammonton*, 351 F.3d 108, 114 (3d Cir. 2003) (applying the "unusually suggestive" standard and requiring more than timing where the interval was not so close).

**C. Plaintiff's timing evidence falls short.**

Here, [number] [days/weeks/months] separated [Plaintiff's] protected activity from the [adverse action]. That interval is far longer than the two days in *Jalil* and is comparable to, or longer than, the intervals this Court has found insufficient. *See LeBoon*, 503 F.3d at 232–33; *Williams*, 380 F.3d at 760. The timing therefore is not unusually suggestive, and Plaintiff must offer additional record evidence of retaliatory motive.

Plaintiff has none. There is no evidence of intervening antagonism, no retaliatory remarks, and no comparator who engaged in similar conduct yet was treated differently. *See Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 281; *Lichtenstein*, 691 F.3d at 307. To the contrary, the record shows that [Defendant] [began the process leading to the challenged action before the protected activity / applied a consistently enforced policy / documented the performance problems before the protected activity]. [Record cites.] An employer that was already contemplating the action before the protected activity cannot be said to have acted because of it. *See Breeden*, 532 U.S. at 272.

Because Plaintiff relies on timing alone and the timing is not unusually suggestive, no reasonable jury could find the causal link that *Krouse*, *Williams*, *Farrell*, and *LeBoon* require. Summary judgment on the retaliation claim should be affirmed.
